metadata.title: Mapping student engagement in creative thinking: An explainable machine learning approach to behavioral heterogeneity

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 creative thinking computer-based assessment process data (from the creative thinking test) and student questionnaire contextual variables for Canada, Germany, and Hong Kong. The analytic sample is restricted to students with valid process data and then further filtered for the predictive task by deleting cases with too few completed tasks (Canada: 10 cases). The manuscript does not report applying PISA sampling/survey weights or replicate weights in the ML pipeline; therefore, it is unclear whether complex survey design features (stratification/clustering) were accounted for in model estimation. For replication, analysts should use the official PISA 2022 student sampling weights (and replicate weights if available) when estimating population-representative effects, but note that the paper’s ML workflow (LASSO feature selection, SMOTE, class weighting, XGBoost, SHAP) is not described as weight-aware.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: plausible_values_handling is 'not_applicable' — the study likely does not analyze cognitive achievement PVs (e.g., it may focus on affective/attitudinal outcomes, curriculum data, or non-ILSA micro-data).

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study extracted valid cases from the PISA 2022 creative thinking CBA process data for three economies (Canada, Germany, Hong Kong). For clustering, it derived four process features per item (scored response/credits, action count, orientation time, processing time) and identified three disengaged behaviors using PISA criteria (rapid responding, relative rapid responding, non-responding) plus the P+>0% method; remaining engaged behaviors were standardized to z-scores. For the predictive analysis, students were classified as disengaged vs engaged based on their most common engagement/disengagement patterns across multiple creative tasks, and contextual questionnaire variables were merged. Variables with missingness >30% were deleted; for remaining variables, hot-deck imputation with KNN was used. Additionally, in Canada, 10 cases were deleted due to too few completed tasks and missing mode.task-level and individual-level factors.

confounders_identified.variable_name: ICT use for school activities outside class

main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost (with LASSO feature selection; SMOTE + class weighting; 80/20 split; 10-fold CV on training). Accuracy: 0.92; Precision: 0.93; Recall: 0.92; F1: 0.93; Specificity: 0.96; AUC: 0.75.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (CBA) data for Canada, the study leveraged self-reported effort (EFFORT1), working in the household (WORKHOME), reading and mathematics achievement, and creative self-efficacy (CREATEFF) to predict engagement vs disengagement across multiple creative tasks, finding that the XGBoost model achieved strong classification performance (Accuracy=0.92, F1=0.93) with effort- and achievement-related factors among the most important predictors. This indicates that strengthening students’ perceived effort and domain competencies (especially reading/mathematics) may help reduce disengagement in creative-thinking tasks, though the study is predictive and does not establish causal effects.

main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost (with LASSO feature selection; SMOTE + class weighting; 80/20 split; 10-fold CV on training). Accuracy: 0.91; Precision: 0.92; Recall: 0.92; F1: 0.92; Specificity: 0.96; AUC: 0.79.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (CBA) data for Germany, the study leveraged mathematics and reading achievement, mathematics self-efficacy (MATHEF21), intended effort (EFFORT2), and working in the household (WORKHOME) to predict engagement vs disengagement across multiple creative tasks, finding that the XGBoost model achieved strong performance (Accuracy=0.91, F1=0.92) and that SHAP-based patterns highlighted both linear and non-linear relationships for key predictors. This indicates that interventions should be context-sensitive—supporting self-efficacy and managing how advanced math exposure is translated into motivation for open-ended creativity—though causality cannot be inferred from the predictive model.

main_findings.performance_metrics: XGBoost (with LASSO feature selection; SMOTE + class weighting; 80/20 split; 10-fold CV on training). Accuracy: 0.87; Precision: 0.87; Recall: 0.87; F1: 0.87; Specificity: 0.93; AUC: 0.78.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 Creative Thinking (CBA) data for Hong Kong, the study leveraged science and reading achievement, parents’ career expectations (PAREXPT), self-reported effort (EFFORT1), and distress from online cyberbullying (ICTDISTR) to predict engagement vs disengagement across multiple creative tasks, finding that the XGBoost model still performed well (Accuracy=0.87, F1=0.87) with SHAP dependence plots indicating threshold and non-linear effects for some predictors. This indicates that reducing psychosocial stressors and supporting family expectations and effort may help sustain engagement in creative tasks, while the results remain correlational/predictive rather than causal.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2022 creative thinking computer-based assessment (CBA) process data and student questionnaire context for three economies (Canada, Germany, Hong Kong; total valid creative-thinking test cases: Canada n=6,794, Germany n=1,692, Hong Kong n=1,661). It first identifies disengaged behaviors (rapid responding, relative rapid responding, non-responding) and uses k-means clustering on four process features (credits, action count, orientation time, processing time) to derive six engagement patterns across tasks. For prediction, students are labeled as engaged vs disengaged based on their most common pattern across multiple creative tasks, and contextual variables are merged; variables with >30% missingness are deleted and remaining missing values are imputed via hot-deck KNN. Using LASSO for feature selection and XGBoost for classification (with SMOTE and class weighting to address ~95/5 imbalance), the models achieve Accuracy/F1 of 0.92/0.93 (Canada), 0.91/0.92 (Germany), and 0.87/0.87 (Hong Kong), with SHAP used for global explainability. Limitations include the lack of reported survey-weight usage and the fact that SHAP explanations support predictive interpretation rather than causal claims.
